doc.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998

chapter: Joining and playing in the Basie band
title: 'Pasadena': passing in arrangements
summary: The band's code word 'Pasadena' meant pass it in, used mostly on outside arrangements.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But many other songs that sounded like that in rehearsal never got played. And we had an expression, if we were rehearsing something and it wasn’t going well, either because it was too busy or the harmonies weren’t right or it sounded amateurish, we had an expression, “Pasadena,” which meant pass it in. And after we worked on that chart for about ten, fifteen minutes, Marshall Royal, who was the straw boss, he’d say “Pasadena.” And I guess this was sort of code terminology so that if the arranger was somebody outside the band, he wouldn’t know what we were talking about, but you’d see all this music converging on one spot, and it was being passed in.

Well they never said that about arrangements by guys in the band. But a lot of people outside the band submitted music, including some seasoned professional arrangers that were supposed to know their craft. And a lot of them would just leave the arrangement at the Basie office and it’d be passed out to the band. And if we shook our heads — sometimes we didn’t even have to wait for Basie. He wouldn’t always rehearse with us. He might be sitting over in a corner smoking a cigar somewhere and reading the paper. And it was sounding pretty corny, we’d look at each other and the next thing would be “Pasadena.” And that would be the end of that.
